energy and the mean stress agree with the PCG result to 1e-6 eV and 2e-7
eV/Angstrom^3.
A deck without `CONSTANT CUTOFF` has A = 0 and keeps the stock diagonal.

# Dipoles from repeated SCF calls
OpenCPMD does not update `ddip%pdipole` in `wfopts`.
The `ddipo` routine updates that electronic polarization, adds the ionic term,
and stores the cell-volume-scaled molecular moment in `dipomod%moment%dmom`.
The molecular-dynamics and property drivers call `ddipo` only on their own
paths, which cpmdc's direct `wfopts` calls do not enter.
Reading either module after an ordinary in-process evaluation would therefore
return stale state.

The dipole patch adds an embed-only request to `wfopts_utils`.
After a converged periodic Gamma-point, non-broken-symmetry evaluation,
`wfopts` calls `ddipo_embed` when the deck requests `DIPOLE DYNAMICS` or
`PROP / DIPOLE MOMENT BERRY`.
`ddipo_embed` is a new entry point of `ddipo_utils` that sets a module flag and
calls `ddipo` with its original argument list.
The flag forces the dipole matrices to be recomputed even when a Wannier
sampling interval would reuse them.
`ddipo` itself keeps the argument list that its eleven callers (`mdclas`,
`mdmain`, `mdshop_cp`, `mm_mdmain`, `mm_mdshop_cp`, `pi_md`, `pi_npt_cpmd`,
`prbomd`, `prcpmd`, `proppt`, and `secder_driver`, which calls it at two sites
for the minimum structure and for the displaced ones) were compiled with, so an
already built tree needs only `ddipo_utils` and `wfopts_utils` recompiled, which
`tools/rebuild_opencpmd_embed.sh` does.
`secder_driver` needs no patch: it passes the same seven arguments, runs only in
a frequency calculation, which an embedded evaluation never enters, and
`embed_force_recompute` stays false there.
An optional argument on `ddipo` would be read by those callers from a
register they never set.
It snapshots `moment%dmom` and marks that evaluation valid.
All other evaluations clear validity.
After an embed teardown, `ddipo` frees its saved maps and starts from the new
basis.
`cpmd.x` leaves the embed request false and retains its original call paths.

The electronic part is a Berry-phase quantity.
The dipole is defined only for a neutral cell, and only modulo the lattice
quantum: moving one electron through a lattice vector changes it by that
vector.
The patch publishes what `ddipo` computes and does not unwrap that jump or
check the net charge.

The k-point orthogonalization patch fixes two heap buffer overflows when `atomwf`
initializes a k-point calculation with more electronic states than atomic
orbitals (`nstate > atwp%nattot`, or `nsup > atwp%nattot` or `nsdown > atwp%nattot`
under `LSD`).
`gs_ortho_c` fills `np * n0` complex entries in `ovlap2_c` and then calls
`mp_sum(smat, 2*np*n0, parai%allgrp)` on a `COMPLEX(real_8)` matrix, which
dispatches to `MPI_Allreduce` with `MPI_DOUBLE_COMPLEX` and reads and overwrites
twice the overlap matrix size.
Changing that count to `np*n0` matches `rgs_c`.
In `atomwf`, passing `zmatat(atwp%nattot, atwp%nattot)` to `gs_ortho_c` also
overflows whenever `nleft > atwp%nattot`, and the `tlsd2` spin-up call passes the
rank-1 slice `c0(:, atwp%nattot+1, ikind)` instead of
`c0(:, atwp%nattot+1:, ikind)`.
The patch allocates a local `smat_c(nleft, MAX(atwp%nattot, nleft))` around each
`gs_ortho_c` call and fixes the spin-up slice.

# Nuclear forces from repeated SCF calls
A live OpenCPMD link evaluates each geometry with fixed nuclei
(`OPTIMIZE WAVEFUNCTION`) and then exports nuclear forces from `coor%fion`, the
same Born-Oppenheimer force definition as a single-point force evaluation after
the SCF (self-consistent field).

On the embed path the Fortran bridge always calls
`embed_set_need_forces(.TRUE.)` before `wfopts`.
The same subroutine calls `embed_set_write_files(.FALSE.)`, so the force call
writes no `RESTART.1`, `LATEST`, `GEOMETRY`, or `GEOMETRY.xyz`.
`cpmd.x` leaves that flag true.
OpenCPMD must be patched so `rwfopt` sets
`tfor = (iprint_force == 1) .OR. embed_need_forces`.
Without that, OpenCPMD zeros `fion` after `forcedr` when `tfor` is false and the
C force buffer stays all zeros even though the energy is finite.
`rwfopt` frees a surviving `fion` before its own `ALLOCATE`, so the bridge's
`IF (ALLOCATED(fion))` guard is optional.

Warm calls (same process, same cell, same method, same elemental composition,
new `ForceInput` positions):

1. First force call of the process: cold setup once, from the in-memory deck.
   The SCF sets `embed_set_warm_orbitals` so a converged `c0` is stored.
   Restore does nothing until that copy exists.
2. Later calls, including a new session and a reordering of the same atomic
   numbers: update `tau0` from C arrays, `phfac`, full SCF from the retained
   orbitals, no second setup.
   An unconverged ODIIS pass does not replace the stored `c0`.
   The same call then continues once with `PCG MINIMIZE` from that previous
   converged copy, and the call still counts as warm.
3. Every call requests forces through
   `embed_set_need_forces` and keeps the deck's `MAXITER`; `tests/test_embed_warm_no_nomore_clamp.py`
   and `tests/test_embed_bomd_force_export.py` guard both.

Wavefunction state (file:wavefunction-state.org) explains what makes a call
cold or warm.

# Why the MPI sentinels stay exported
The export list hides every other symbol of the archives except the MPI Fortran
sentinels: `USE mpi` gives OpenCPMD's objects the COMMON blocks behind
`MPI_IN_PLACE`, `MPI_BOTTOM`, and `MPI_STATUS_IGNORE` (`mpi_fortran_*_` in Open
MPI, `mpipriv1_` and its siblings in MPICH), and the MPI library recognizes a
sentinel by the address of its own block.
Hidden in `libcpmdc`, they became private copies, and every `MPI_IN_PLACE`
collective sent the zeros of that copy instead of the data: with Open MPI 5 the
first SCF faulted in `gorder`, after `my_allgather_i` had overwritten the
plane-wave counts with zeros.
Kept global, they resolve to one block per process.
The serial library does not link that archive, so those blocks are not in it.
The ELF version script can name them anyway: a global pattern exports a symbol
that is present and does not require it.
ld64's export list requires every literal name to be defined while wildcard
entries match only defined symbols, so every sentinel uses a wildcard pattern
(letting either Open MPI or MPICH link) and the macOS list adds them only when
OpenCPMD is linked.


## File: docs/orgmode/explanation/routes.org

A host can reach CPMD through several layers.
The default local interface is the in-process session API:
=Session.calculate_au()= for atomic-unit arrays, or
=cpmdc_session_calculate_result()= for Cap'n Proto messages.
The default remote interface is rgpot's Cap'n Proto RPC over =CPMDPot=.
i-PI is an optional rgpot protocol frontend over potentials; protocol
frontends do not belong inside an engine library.  In an rgpot build with
the RPC stack, =rgpot-ipi-driver= selects =CPMDPot= for
=--pot "CPMD params FILE"= and for `-m CPMD -o params=FILE`.
Pass =--preserve-open-cell= for CPMD so a singular cell is passed through
instead of padded.  The
i-PI migration status (file:../howto/socket-drivers.org) records that
route.  =cpmdc-ipi= and =cpmdc-ipi-c= remain compatibility fallbacks.

The measurements below compare the two original execution routes.
The file route writes a deck, starts `cpmd.x` for each force call, and reads
the energy and forces back from CPMD's output files.
The in-process route loads `libcpmdc` once and calls it; CPMD runs inside the
host, and geometry and forces move as C arrays.
Both run the same OpenCPMD source on the same input.
They differ in what a call costs, in how the wavefunction of one call reaches
the next, and in what can go wrong.

The numbers on this page come from one study: a 7-atom Si3N4 cluster, BLYP at
70 Ry in a 14 Angstrom cube, Kleinman-Bylander pseudopotentials, orbital
convergence 1e-5, driven by eOn.
The file route was eOn's `ext_pot` potential with a wrapper around
`mpirun cpmd.x`; the in-process route was eOn's `RGPOT` potential with
`cpmdc`.
Each CPMD instance ran on 16 MPI ranks unless a row says otherwise.

# What one call costs

| Route | Per call |
|-------+----------|
| file | 3.7 s fixed, plus 0.54 s per SCF iteration (least-squares fit over 20 calls) |
| file, geometry unchanged | 4.3 s for a single SCF iteration |
| in-process, ODIIS | 0.64 s per SCF step, no fixed part after the first call |
| in-process, `PCG MINIMIZE` | 1.26 s per SCF step |

The fixed 3.7 s of the file route is the price of a new process: `mpirun`
start, CPMD's setup of the plane-wave basis and the pseudopotentials, and
reading a 23 MB `RESTART.1` before the first SCF iteration.
The in-process route pays that setup once per session and then only the SCF.
A file-route call cannot get cheaper than its fixed part, whatever the
geometry.

# How the wavefunction travels
The file route starts each call from a saved `RESTART.1`.
In the study, every converged call stored its restart file in a pool with its
positions, and a new call loaded the one whose geometry was nearest.
The in-process route keeps the orbitals of the previous call in memory on
every rank and starts the next SCF from them.

The two policies behave differently in a nudged elastic band.
There eOn gives each image its own file-route potential, so the nearest
pooled geometry is usually the same image one band step earlier, a few
hundredths of an Angstrom away.
The in-process client evaluates the images one after another, so each call
starts from the previous image, a neighbour along the path.

| OCI-NEB run, same settings | File route | In-process route |
|------------------------------------+------------+------------------|
| force calls | 364 | 363 |
| SCF iterations per call | 13.5 | 30.6 |
| CPMD instances at once | 7, of 6 ranks each | 1, of 16 ranks |
| wall time from first to last band | 3798 s | 12908 s |
| effective wall time per call | 10 s | 35 s |
| barrier | 0.243388 eV | 0.243459 eV |

The barriers agree to 0.07 meV, and the call counts to one call.
The in-process run lost on two counts that the per-call table does not show:
its warm start came from a neighbouring image, and its images ran in series
on one CPMD instance while the file route ran seven at once.
It also used `PCG MINIMIZE` on every call, at about two energy evaluations per
SCF step.
A single-image search suffers less from the warm-start difference: a dimer
search on the in-process route took 212 calls at 15.5 s per call and 17.2 SCF
iterations per call.

Two changes close most of the gap, and `cpmdc` already provides the first:
calculator groups (`cpmdc_bind_calculator`) run one CPMD instance per image
side by side, and ODIIS instead of `PCG MINIMIZE` halves the cost of a warm
SCF step (see choosing the optimiser (file:../howto/wavefunction-optimiser.org)).

# What each route has to guard against

| Hazard | File route | In-process route |
|--------+------------+------------------|
| two calls sharing file names in one directory | real: each potential object needs its own directory | none: no deck or result files are read |
| reading a stale `GEOMETRY` as this call's forces | real: remove it before each run | none: forces come from `coor%fion` |
| an unconverged SCF that still prints `TOTAL ENERGY` | real: check for `NO CONVERGENCE` | reported as a failed call |
| a shared restart pool pruned by another client | real: tolerate a vanished entry | none |
| a CPMD stop | `cpmd.x` ends and the wrapper sees a failed run | `cpmd_stopgm_hook` returns nonzero, the call's wavefunction and forces are undefined, and the next call sets CPMD up again. More than one rank aborts the others |
| rank consistency under `mpirun` | none: the host runs as one process | the host must take the parent rank's result and finalize MPI |
| the method deck | written by the host, whole | rendered from `CPMDParams`; defaults apply to what the message leaves out |

The file route can be made safe; it cannot be made cheap.
The in-process route removes the fixed cost and the file hazards, and moves
the burden to getting the message and the MPI handling right.

# Both routes give the same answers
Every energy compared across the two routes and the two optimisers agreed
within the orbital convergence tolerance.
A 4-rank in-process single point of the cluster's reference geometry gave
-1396.269515581643 eV on all four ranks.
The optimiser and the warm-start policy change the path to the converged
wavefunction, not the converged state.


## File: docs/orgmode/explanation/simd-paths.org

# Paths
The force path of `cpmdc` has no hot numeric kernel.
The C sources compile a deck and read Cap'n Proto messages.
The optional plane-wave scaling scaffold (`-Dwith_pwscale=true`, see
the rank how-to (file:../howto/pwscale-ranks.org)) has kernels, and it is not
on the force path.
The Fortran sources are the embedding bridge into OpenCPMD.
There is no AVX-512 path, no AVX2 path, and no NEON path in this repository.
Every translation unit compiles for x86-64 (v1) on x86_64 and armv8-a on
aarch64.
The Meson build passes `-march=x86-64` or `-march=armv8-a`. conda-forge
compilers export `CFLAGS=-march=nocona`, and Meson appends that environment
after its own arguments, so the later `-march` would win.
`scripts/with_baseline_flags.sh` drops `-march` and the other ISA selectors from
`CFLAGS`, `CXXFLAGS`, `FFLAGS`, and `FCFLAGS` before `meson setup`.
The Pixi test tasks source that script.
The build does not pass `-march=native`, `-mavx*`, or `-march=x86-64-v3`.

OpenCPMD is Fortran.
`cpmdc` adds no runtime dispatch inside it.
The portable configure files in `tools/` are the build target.
See the archive how-to (file:../howto/opencpmd-archive.org).

# How selection works
There is no path table and no `CPMDC_SIMD` variable.
`cpmdc` does not read `CPMDC_SIMD`.
An environment value cannot select a kernel this library does not ship.
The baseline compile is the only path in the C and Fortran sources.

The minimage subproject is a Rust static library linked into `libcpmdc`.
It compiles its AVX, AVX2, and AVX-512 kernels with
`#[target_feature]` and calls one only after `std::is_x86_feature_detected!`
reports the features it needs.
The Rust standard library linked with it also contains the `memchr` AVX2
searcher. libstd builds `memchr` without its `std` feature, so
`Finder::is_available()` returns false and the searcher is never called.
The standard library feature detection reads `XCR0` with `_xgetbv` only after
the processor identification instruction (CPUID) reports XSAVE and OSXSAVE.
The test suite calls only the one-pair displacement, which takes the scalar path
on every CPU, so it runs no dispatched kernel.

OpenBLAS and the Fastest Fourier Transform in the West (FFTW), which an OpenCPMD
link pulls in, select kernels at run time when built with `DYNAMIC_ARCH` and
with FFTW's single instruction multiple data (SIMD) codelets.
Those instructions sit in those libraries, not in a `cpmdc` symbol.
The instruction set architecture (ISA) audit allowlist names no `cpmdc` symbol.
Its symbol rules name the minimage kernels, the `memchr` searcher functions
`find_impl` and `find_prefilter_impl`, and `_xgetbv` from `core`.
Each rule lists the features those functions may use and the run-time check that
guards them.
The allowlist names OpenBLAS or libgfortran only when a build links that library
statically into an audited artefact.
The default link is dynamic, so the allowlist has no vendored path.

Dispatched kernels elsewhere in this set of libraries follow the cluster-pair
layout of Páll and Hess, Comput.
Phys.
Commun. 184, 2641 (2013),
doi:10.1016/j.cpc.2013.06.003. One binary per microarchitecture belongs in EESSI (Dröge et al., Softw. Pract. Exp. 53, 176 (2023), doi:10.1002/spe.3075).

# Bit-identical results
The same input gives the same output bits on every baseline build of the C and
Fortran sources, because they have one code path.
C and Fortran compile with `-ffp-contract=off`.
On MSVC the matching flag is `/fp:precise`, which does not contract.
The compiler does not fuse a multiply and an add, so a result does not depend on
whether the build host would have contracted those operations.
Reductions in this repository do not split a sum into partials.
Sources do not call a fused multiply-add intrinsic.

Three exceptions sit outside that guarantee.
Cell angles in `src/cpmdc_params.c` call libm `cos` when a six-element cell is
written from degrees.
That `cos` is libm, not an in-house polynomial, and glibc can pick an
implementation at run time, so those characters of a rendered deck can differ
across libm builds.
OpenBLAS, FFTW, and OpenCPMD's own math are not compiled by `cpmdc`.
Their kernels are not bit-identical across CPUs. minimage is built with `cpmdc`
but picks its kernel at run time.
Its scalar orthorhombic kernel adds the squared components as
`(x*x + y*y) + z*z` and its AVX kernel as `x*x + (y*y + z*z)`, so a distance it
returns can differ in the last bit between CPUs. glibc `exp`, `log`, and `pow`
have the same kind of runtime choice.
`cpmdc` does not call them for a value it defines.


## File: docs/orgmode/explanation/wavefunction-state.org

A force call on a geometry close to the previous one should not start its
self-consistent field (SCF) from scratch.
The converged orbitals of the last call, `c0` in OpenCPMD, are a far better
starting point than atomic orbitals, and keeping them in memory is the main
reason to run CPMD inside the host.
This page follows `c0` from call to call.

# Cold and warm calls
The process keeps the converged orbitals, the cell, and the method that produced
them.
Each session keeps a counter of its own successful calls.

| Call | Condition | What runs |
|------+-----------+-----------|
| cold | first call of the process, or a changed functional, deck, cell, cutoff, charge, multiplicity, atom count, or elemental composition | the full CPMD setup on the composed deck, then the SCF from CPMD's initial guess, or from `RESTART` when the deck has `RESTART WAVEFUNCTION` |
| warm | a previous success in this process kept the same functional, deck, cell, cutoff, charge, multiplicity, and elemental composition, including a new session or a reordering of those atomic numbers, and the geometry is within `CPMDC_WARM_RMSD` (default 0.15 Angstrom) of a stored geometry | new positions into `tau0`, `phfac`, then the SCF from the stored `c0` |
| deck guess without full setup | the same basis and cell match as a warm call, but every stored geometry lies beyond `CPMDC_WARM_RMSD` | new positions into `tau0`, `phfac`, then the SCF from the deck's guess without re-running CPMD setup |
| in place | as warm or deck guess without full setup, on a constant-cutoff deck under `CPMDC_CELL_IN_PLACE` whose new periodic cell lies within the strain limit of the setup cell (`has_cell` and `embed_saved_has_cell` are both non-zero) | the new cell on the setup's plane waves, then as warm within `CPMDC_WARM_RMSD` or from the deck's guess beyond it |

A cell counts as unchanged when every component of `ForceInput.box` matches the
stored cell within 1e-8 Angstrom, and when both calls agree on having a box at
all (a step without a cell matches only when the latched state also has no
cell; `CPMDC_CELL_IN_PLACE` does not apply there because
`embed_cell_moves_in_place` returns false when `has_cell` is 0).
A new session has no cell of its own yet, so that comparison uses the cell
stored with the orbitals.
The cutoff matches within 1e-8 Rydberg.
The elemental composition is the count of each atomic number.
Reordering the same atoms keeps that composition.
The charge and the multiplicity belong to the same match.
A failed warm call leaves the counter where it was, so the next call is warm
again; a failed cold call clears the stored results.
An SCF that does not converge does not replace the stored orbitals.
When ODIIS exhausts `MAXITER`, the same call continues once with `PCG MINIMIZE`.
That pass restores the previous converged `c0` when a converged copy is already
stored, and it still counts as warm.
When the continuation runs out too, the call fails, and the message in
`CPMDCResult.message` and `cpmdc_last_error()` names the minimizer of each pass,
the iteration each one stopped at, `MAXITER`, and the final `gemax` against
`CONVERGENCE ORBITALS`:
CPMD SCF did not converge: PCG MINIMIZE stopped at iteration 2 of MAXITER 2 with gemax 1.107715E-02 above CONVERGENCE ORBITALS 1.000000E-05, after ODIIS stopped at iteration 2 of MAXITER 2
That is water with BLYP at 50 Ry under `MAXITER 2`, the case
`tests/test_scf_unconverged.c` runs against OpenCPMD.
A host that prints `cpmdc`'s message, as rgpot's `CPMD engine failed:` does,
shows these fields unchanged.
A `stopgm` during the call is not that failure: the wavefunction, forces, and
module state of the call are undefined, `cpmdc` drops the stored orbitals and
the warm cell, and the next call runs setup again.
With more than one MPI rank, `cpmdc` aborts the other ranks.

# Where the orbitals are kept
`opencpmd_embed_rwfopt.patch` adds a module-level copy of `c0` to
`rwfopt_utils`.
At the end of `rwfopt`, every rank saves its own slice of `c0` when
`embed_warm_orbitals` is true and `ropt_mod%convwf` is true.
A call that does not converge leaves the previous copy in place.
A failed store allocation calls `stopgm`.
`cpmdc` sets `embed_warm_orbitals` on every SCF, including the first.
Restore does nothing until a converged copy exists, so the first call still
starts from CPMD's guess and stores `c0` only if that SCF converges.
On a later call, `rwfopt` copies the saved `c0` in before `initrun`.
`rinitwf` then returns after the phase factors, so it does not build a guess,
and the density `initrun` builds comes from those orbitals.
A restart read inside `initrun` can replace `c0`, so `rwfopt` copies the saved
orbitals in again after `initrun` when the shape still matches.
A different shape calls `stopgm` and names `embed_reset_warm_orbitals`.
`cpmdc` makes that call when the functional, the deck, the cutoff, the cell, the
charge, the multiplicity, the atom count, or the elemental composition changes,
before `rwfopt` runs; a cell that moves in place keeps the orbitals.
The SCF then runs to the orbital convergence threshold with the full `MAXITER`
budget of the deck; a warm call is a complete SCF from a better start, not a
shortened one.

`opencpmd_converged_state.patch` makes the saved copy trustworthy.
In stock OpenCPMD, `updwf` applies an optimiser step to `c0` before it checks
convergence, so the orbitals left behind after the last iteration have moved one
step past the ones that produced the reported energy and forces.
The patch checks convergence first and updates only unconverged orbitals, so the
saved `c0` is the state that `forcedr` used.
Steepest descent with `iproj <= 1` sets `gemax` above the threshold before that
check: those steps do not converge on `gemax`.

# Orbitals per key
One calculator often evaluates several calculations in turn: the images of a
band on fewer calculators than images, or the beads of a ring polymer.
With one stored copy, each SCF starts from the orbitals of whichever calculation
ran last on that calculator, which for a ring is a neighbouring bead rather than
the same bead one step earlier.
`cpmdc_session_select_orbitals()` names the calculation the next evaluations
belong to.
The call records the key, and the evaluation selects it.
A key named and then replaced before an evaluation parks nothing.
`opencpmd_embed_rwfopt.patch` keeps a table of stored `c0` copies, one per key,
beside the store `rwfopt` restores from.
Selecting another key parks the `c0` of the key being left, including a stale
copy from an unconverged pass, and moves the copy parked under the new key
into the store.
A partial copy from an unconverged pass is not parked.
`cpmdc_session_copy_orbitals()` duplicates one key's converged orbitals, and
the geometry they converged at, into another key, replacing that key's
previous copy.
The selected key stays selected.
When the destination is the selected key, its live store is replaced
immediately.
A key with no converged orbitals is refused.
A donor whose last pass did not converge is refused as well, whether that
copy is the live store or a parked slot, and a copy onto the same key is
refused too.
Selecting that key again, or a warm start that adopts the parked slot, keeps
the refusal.
Every rank of a calculator names the same keys.
Every rank of a calculator selects the same key, and each rank parks its own
slice of `c0`.
`CPMDC_ORBITAL_SLOT_LIMIT`, a positive integer, is the most of those parked
copies.
A park that would pass it fails the evaluation or the copy, the result names
the variable through `cpmdc_last_error()`, and the copies already stored stay
in the table.
Lowering the limit does not drop a copy that is already parked.
Unset, the table is unbounded.
A value that is not a positive integer fails the call.
A basis change frees the table with the store, since every copy in it has the
shape of the old basis.
It does so before the key of the new call is selected, so a limit that the old
basis filled does not refuse the first key of the new one.
A session that never selects a key keeps one stored copy.

# Distance limit
Every stored and parked `c0` carries the geometry it converged at, the Angstrom
positions the caller passed.
Before each SCF, `embed_choose_warm_start_metric_v2` measures the
root-mean-square distance per atom from the new geometry to each of them,
without alignment.
The nearest one starts the SCF.
It is either the store, which holds the selected key's own copy or, when that
key has none, the copy of the key last left, or another key's parked copy, which
is copied so the donor keeps its own.
When that distance exceeds `CPMDC_WARM_RMSD` (default 0.15 Angstrom), the SCF
starts from the deck's guess without full CPMD setup instead, a third case that
is neither a warm start from stored orbitals nor a cold start after full setup,
and the stored copy of that call is dropped.
A negative limit starts from the store at any distance.
When the native `tclust` flag is false, the metric uses minimage's Euclidean
closest lattice image in the native cell, including skew cells.
A true `tclust` flag selects absolute Cartesian distances even when a cell is
supplied.
The parser sets this flag for `CLUSTER`, `SURFACE`, `POLYMER` or `SYMMETRY 0`; a
`POISSON` keyword alone does not establish it.
Coordinates are compared in species order without rotation or alignment.
A cell or boundary-model change invalidates every stored orbital state,
including when the distance limit is negative.
A cell that moves in place is not such a change: the distances then use the
setup cell, the cell of the plane waves the orbitals are written on.

The default comes from the Si3N4 BLYP 70 Ry band (7 atoms, 14 Angstrom cell,
ODIIS, 4 ranks per calculation).
One process makes two calls.
The second sits a set distance along the band from the first and starts from the
first call's orbitals or from the deck's atomic guess.
Five starting images, means over them per call:
| RMSD (Angstrom) | SCF steps, warm | SCF steps, guess | wall saved by the warm start (s) |
|-----------------+-----------------+------------------+----------------------------------|
|           0.047 |            24.0 |             32.4 |                                  |
|           0.116 |            29.2 |             33.2 |                              4.5 |
|           0.149 |            32.4 |             33.0 |                              2.1 |
|           0.167 |            33.8 |             33.4 |                              1.2 |
|           0.186 |            35.4 |             33.0 |                             -0.4 |
|           0.233 |            37.6 |             32.8 |                             -2.4 |
|      0.46 (3)   |            47.7 |             37.7 |                                  |
|      0.9 to 3.1 |      36 to 283 |         19 to 52 |                                  |
Next to an endpoint the guess is already close (19 to 26 steps): a warm start
there gains at most 3 steps and loses from 0.12 Angstrom on.
Mid-path images gain up to 27 steps at 0.05 Angstrom.
The 0.46 row has three starting images; the last row covers the warm starts from
images 0, 4 and 8 to every image that far away.
The deck's guess, not the simple guess (`inwfun 3`) a process that holds
orbitals otherwise takes, is the start past the limit: the simple guess took 65
to 205 steps on the same images where the deck's took 37 to 52.
A band step capped at 0.1 Angstrom per atom stays inside the limit, so an image
that returns to its own key is warm.
`CPMDC_SCF_STEPS=1` prints the start of every call.

# Extrapolation between calls
A warm start is a zeroth-order guess: the next SCF starts from the last
converged orbitals as they are.
Along a trajectory with equal time steps, a combination of the orbitals of the
earlier steps predicts the next ones better.
Car-Parrinello molecular dynamics (CPMD) does this in its own Born-Oppenheimer
molecular dynamics (BO-MD) with `EXTRAPOLATE WFN`, and the always stable
predictor-corrector (ASPC) of Kolafa (J. Comput. Chem. 25, 335 (2004),
doi:10.1002/jcc.10385) is one of its coefficient sets. CP2K extrapolates by default, with ASPC of order 3 (`FORCE_EVAL/DFT/QS EXTRAPOLATION`), and Quantum ESPRESSO offers first- and second-order extrapolation of the wavefunctions after Arias, Payne, and Joannopoulos (Phys. Rev. B 45, 1538 (1992), doi:10.1103/PhysRevB.45.1538).

OpenCPMD turns the keyword off in a wavefunction optimisation, which is the job
a host-driven call runs.
`tools/opencpmd_embed_extrapolate.patch` keeps the request and lets `rwfopt` act
on it when the orbitals stay in memory.
After a converged SCF, the orbitals go into the store as before.
At the start of the next call, `rwfopt` pushes that copy into a ring of `order`
entries and calls CPMD's `extrapwf`, which builds the prediction, rotates the
earlier sets onto the newest one by their overlap, and orthonormalises the
result.
The SCF then runs from that prediction to the same convergence threshold.
The ring is one per process, not one per key, so a key change, an unconverged
pass, or a start past the distance limit empties it.
An unconverged pass empties it even when a converged copy was already stored.
`opencpmd_embed_rwfopt.patch` marks that copy stale on that branch, and
`opencpmd_embed_extrapolate.patch` calls `embed_break_history` there.
Before those hunks, that pass left the ring in place, and only a first
unconverged pass, the one that keeps a partial copy, cleared it.
The extrapolation how-to (file:../howto/extrapolate-orbitals.org) lists those
events.

A water molecule with the Becke-Lee-Yang-Parr (BLYP) functional at 50 Ry, on one
rank, makes the comparison.
`cpmd.x` ran the deck of `tests/water_aspc_params.capnp.txt` as BO-MD for 40
steps of 10 atomic time units.
The library route ran the same 41 geometries from `cpmd.x`'s trajectory, one
call each, in one process.
SCF iterations count steps 1 to 40; the first SCF, cold on both routes, took 18.

| Route | Start of each SCF | SCF iterations | Wall time (s) |
|-------+-------------------+----------------+---------------|
| `cpmd.x` | previous orbitals | 441 | 376.1 |
| `cpmd.x` | ASPC, order 4 | 292 | 263.4 |
| library | previous orbitals | 440 | 392.6 |
| library | ASPC, order 4 | 297 | 267.7 |

The library energies match `cpmd.x`'s `ENERGIES` file within 1.9e-10 Hartree on
steps 1 to 40 of both runs.
Library wall times cover the whole test process, setup included.
For `cpmd.x`, the table gives its reported elapsed time.
Over the first 12 steps, the case `tests/test_extrapolate_wfn.c` runs, the SCF
iteration count is 88 on both routes with ASPC and 124 without.
Over 40 steps, the library route takes 5 more iterations than `cpmd.x` with ASPC
and one fewer without, while the energies of the two routes differ from the
tenth decimal on.

# Cell changes at a constant cutoff
A plane wave is a reciprocal lattice vector G(m) = 2 pi m H^-1 for integer m and
lattice rows H, so the set of m inside the cutoff sphere, and with it the layout
of `c0`, belongs to the cell of the setup.
The penalty of `CONSTANT CUTOFF` leaves the components above E0 + 2 sigma
empty in any cell.
While the setup's set of m holds every m whose G in the new cell lies below
E0 + 2 sigma, the setup's plane waves span every occupied component of the new
cell, and the stored orbitals still fit.
With T = H_setup^-1 H_new, the squared length of G(m) in the setup cell is at
most the largest eigenvalue of T T^T times its length in the new cell, so
`cpmdc` asks that this eigenvalue times E0 + 2 sigma stay within the
wavefunction cutoff, and four times as much within the density cutoff.

`CPMDC_CELL_IN_PLACE` turns the move on and bounds the principal strain from
the setup cell, the largest stretch or shrink of a length.
A cell within it goes into `metr_com%ht`, and OpenCPMD's `newcell` rescales the
G vectors, the structure factors, and the pseudopotential tables, as OpenCPMD's
own variable-cell dynamics does each step.
The SCF then starts from the stored orbitals and the `EXTRAPOLATE WFN` history.
The move also asks for the Gamma point, norm-conserving pseudopotentials, a
periodic deck, the lattice class of the setup (a cube that stays a cube, an
orthorhombic cell, or `CELL VECTORS`), and the same method otherwise.
A cell past the limit, or one that fails a condition, sets CPMD up again, and
the strain is measured from that new setup cell.

The plane waves between E0 + 2 sigma and the cutoff are then those of the setup
cell rather than of the new one, which moves the energy and the stress away
from those of a new setup in proportion to the strain.
On 32 waters at a 100 Ry cutoff with E0 = 85 Ry and sigma = 4.25 Ry, a 1%
stretch in place differs from a new setup by 3.3 meV in the energy, 0.08
meV/Angstrom in the forces, and 32 bar in the pressure.
The tail of erf reaches further below E0 at a wider sigma: the one-water deck
at 40 Ry with E0 = 30 Ry and the default sigma of 3 Ry differs by about 3 meV,
1.5 meV/Angstrom, and 3e-6 eV/Angstrom^3 for the same stretch.
Within one setup, the energies of the moved cells lie on one smooth surface
whose derivative is the stress, which the `python-pytest` case
`test_the_constant_cutoff_stress_is_the_volume_derivative_of_the_energy` checks.

# What clears the orbitals

| Event | Why |
|-------+-----|
| a cell change, unless it moves in place | the plane-wave basis depends on the cell, so the stored coefficients no longer fit |
| a cutoff change | the plane-wave basis changes, so the stored coefficients no longer fit |
| a change of atom count or elemental composition, or of charge or multiplicity | those inputs set the number of states, and a restored `c0` of another shape calls `stopgm` |
| `cpmdc_session_set_params()` or `cpmdc_session_configure()` when the functional, cutoff, charge, multiplicity, or deck differs | the next evaluation drops the orbitals; the call itself keeps them |
| a new session with the same functional, deck, cutoff, cell, charge, multiplicity, and elemental composition | reuses the stored orbitals and skips setup |
| a new session whose functional, deck, cutoff, cell, charge, multiplicity, or elemental composition differs | the next evaluation drops the stored orbitals and runs setup |
| a one-shot or global call (`cpmdc_set_params()`, `cpmdc_energy*()`, `cpmdc_calculate_result()`) whose basis differs from the stored one | that call runs setup; a matching basis reuses the orbitals |
| `stopgm` returns through `cpmd_stopgm_hook` | the call continued past a failed check, so the stored orbitals are not a result |

A topology change is refused outright rather than treated as cold: the atom
count and the elemental composition belong to the session.
A reordering of those atomic numbers stays on the session.
A new session with that composition keeps the stored orbitals.
An evaluation whose positions match the previous successful call on that
session, including that reordering, returns the stored energy and forces.

An evaluation that needs a second setup, for a basis that differs from the first
or after a `stopgm`, tears the first one down in the same process.
The teardown frees the module arrays, communicators, and first-call state of
that setup (`embed_teardown_state` from `tools/opencpmd_embed_teardown.patch`),
and the new setup gives the energies of a fresh process.
Resetting the embed after a failed call tears down the same way.
`tistart` runs once per process: OpenCPMD executes `STOP` on a second call.

# The RESTART file
A library force call writes no `RESTART.1`, `LATEST`, `GEOMETRY`, or
`GEOMETRY.xyz`.
The orbitals for the next call stay in memory.
`cpmd.x` writes those files.
A cold library call reads a `RESTART.1` only when the deck asks for
`RESTART WAVEFUNCTION`.
`cpmdc` turns off CPMD's restart of coordinates, velocities, and the stored
geometry before every SCF.
The host owns the geometry, and a `RESTART COORDINATES` in the deck would
otherwise overwrite the step's positions.

To seed a cold start from an earlier run with a new geometry, patch the
positions of a `RESTART.1` with `cpmdc-restart patch-positions`.
It rewrites only the coordinate records and copies the wavefunction records
unchanged; the deck then needs `RESTART WAVEFUNCTION`.

`cpmdc-restart` and `cpmdc_restart_write_path()` replace a `RESTART` file in
one step, so a `cpmd.x` or a library call that opens it at the same time reads
the previous file or the finished one, never part of the new one.
The image goes to a short-named temporary file next to the effective
destination. A new destination is opened with mode 0666 under the umask as a
plain `fopen` would; replacement keeps the destination's existing mode.
On POSIX, when `RESTART` is a symbolic link, as in CPMD's
`RESTART -> RESTART.1` convention, the target is replaced and the link
survives. A dangling link, whose target is not there yet, is resolved hop
by hop to the end of the chain, even past the first missing name, and the
real end is created there: a relative target at each hop is taken from the
directory that holds that hop's link, and the new file takes mode 0666
under the umask, as `fopen` did. While it walks, the writer holds an
`O_DIRECTORY` descriptor for the parent of the destination and one for the
directory that contained each symlink it followed, and it records that
symlink's device, inode, and target text. Immediately before `renameat` it
reads those descriptors again with `fstatat` and `AT_SYMLINK_NOFOLLOW`. If
any followed symlink is no longer that same link, or the final component
is no longer the absent name or the same file that was resolved, the write
fails, the temporary file is removed, and nothing is renamed. A loop, or a
link that cannot be read, is left in place and the write fails.

That check and the rename are not one operation. POSIX has no call that
renames a file only when a whole symlink chain is unchanged, so a full
guarantee is not available. The `renameat` uses the directory descriptor
taken during resolution, which pins that directory inode: replacing an
earlier path component afterwards does not redirect the write onto the
replacement. On Linux, when the headers and kernel provide `renameat2` with
`RENAME_NOREPLACE`, an absent final name that appears in the gap is left
alone and the write fails. If that operation is unavailable or rejected,
the writer falls back to plain `renameat`; a name that appears in the gap
can then be overwritten. When the resolved destination is an existing
file, the last check and the `renameat` are also two calls, and a
substitution of that directory entry in the gap can be overwritten.
Windows resolves none of this: the destination is written as given, with
no symlink handling at all.
The writer flushes that file and syncs it with `fsync`, renames it over the
destination, and syncs the directory with `fsync`, so the new name also
survives a crash.
On Windows, `_commit` flushes the file and `MoveFileEx` with
`MOVEFILE_REPLACE_EXISTING` and `MOVEFILE_WRITE_THROUGH` replaces the
destination.
A failure before the rename removes the temporary file and leaves the old
`RESTART` in place.
A directory that cannot be synced is reported as a failure even though the new
file is already in place; a filesystem that cannot sync a directory at all
(`EINVAL`) is not.
Only a crash before the rename leaves a `.tmp.` file behind, and it can be
deleted.

# The optimiser on a warm start
A warm start changes how far the SCF has to go, not how it gets there.
CPMD's optimiser choice then decides the cost: ODIIS reuses its history of
residuals, while `PCG MINIMIZE` runs a line minimisation per step.
On the Si3N4 cluster of the route comparison (file:routes.org), the same
minimisation took 515 SCF steps at 1.26 s with `PCG MINIMIZE` and 296 steps at
0.64 s with ODIIS, to the same minimum.


## File: docs/orgmode/howto/ase.org

`cpmdc.ase.CPMDCCalculator` is an ASE calculator that evaluates each step in the
Python process, through one cpmdc session.
Set `atoms.calc` to it as to any other ASE calculator: ASE's optimizers, cell
filters, molecular dynamics, and trajectory files use it unchanged.
Importing `cpmdc.ase` registers `CPMDCCalculator` under `"cpmdc"` with
`ase.calculators.calculator.register_calculator_class`, so
`get_calculator_class("cpmdc")` returns it, and an installed package also
exposes `cpmdc.ase` in the `ase.plugins` entry-point group.
ASE releases that ship `ase._4.plugins` (3.29 and later) list the calculator in
`ase._4.plugins.plugins.calculators` whichever of `cpmdc.ase` and `ase._4.plugins`
is imported first; earlier releases have no plugin API and use only the registry.
It starts no `cpmd.x` process and writes no input file.
Call cpmdc from Python (file:python.org) covers `Session` and `Potential`,
the same library without ASE.

# Make the parameters files
The calculator takes the method from a serialized `CPMDParams` message: the
functional, the cutoff, the charge, the multiplicity, the pseudopotentials, and
the boundary conditions of an isolated system.
Write a CPMDParams message (file:write-cpmdparams.org) explains the text
form.
These commands encode the isolated and the periodic water of a checkout at
`$CPMDC` into the working directory:

schema=$(python3 -c "import cpmdc; print(cpmdc.find_schema())")
capnp encode "$schema" CPMDParams < "$CPMDC/tests/water_blyp_params.capnp.txt" > water.params.bin
capnp encode "$schema" CPMDParams < "$CPMDC/tests/water_blyp_periodic_params.capnp.txt" > water.periodic.bin

`water.params.bin` is one molecule with `SYMMETRY 0` and the Hockney Poisson
solver.
`water.periodic.bin` is a simple cubic cell, `SYMMETRY 1`, which gives a stress
tensor.
The examples on this page run on the reference evaluator of the default build
and of the wheel.
On OpenCPMD they need `CPMDC_LIBRARY` to name the build and `CPMDC_PSEUDO_DIR`
to name the pseudopotential directory.

# Evaluate a structure
from ase import Atoms
from cpmdc.ase import CPMDCCalculator

water = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.1173], [0.0, 0.7572, -0.4692], [0.0, -0.7572, -0.4692]]
atoms = Atoms("OHH", positions=water)
with CPMDCCalculator("water.params.bin") as calc:
    atoms.calc = calc
    print(atoms.get_potential_energy())
    print(atoms.get_forces())
    print(calc.todict())

`params` is the path of a `CPMDParams` file or its bytes, and the calculator
reads the file once, when the parameter is set.
`library` is the path of `libcpmdc`; without it the calculator searches the
places that Call cpmdc from Python (file:python.org) lists.
One step computes the energy, the forces, and the stress when the step has one,
so `get_forces` after `get_potential_energy` does not evaluate again:

| Property | ASE call | Unit | Free boundaries | Periodic cell |
|----------+----------+------+-----------------+---------------|
| `energy` | `get_potential_energy()` | eV | yes | yes |
| `free_energy` | `get_potential_energy(force_consistent=True)` | eV | equals `energy` | equals `energy` |
| `forces` | `get_forces()` | eV/Angstrom, shape  | yes | yes |
| `stress` | `get_stress()` | eV/Angstrom^3, Voigt  | raises `PropertyNotImplementedError` | yes, unless the deck is isolated or `CPMDC_STRESS=0` |
| `dipole` | `get_dipole_moment()` | e*Angstrom, shape  | raises `PropertyNotImplementedError` | yes for a supported deck that requests Berry dipole evaluation |
| `energies`, `magmom`, `magmoms`, `charges` | `get_property(name)` | | raises `PropertyNotImplementedError` | raises `PropertyNotImplementedError` |

`free_energy` is the potential energy of the step, because the library does not
separate an electronic entropy.
The library returns no atomic energies, charges, or magnetic moments.
`implemented_properties` lists `dipole` because linked OpenCPMD can deliver it.
It raises `PropertyNotImplementedError` when the current step cannot.

A valid dipole requires a periodic Gamma-point, non-broken-symmetry OpenCPMD
deck with `DIPOLE DYNAMICS` or `PROP / DIPOLE MOMENT BERRY`.
The reference evaluator, isolated and k-point decks, and decks without either
request do not return a dipole.
A deck that combines `DIPOLE DYNAMICS` with `KPOINTS` is rejected when the
calculator opens it, with an error that names both, because OpenCPMD stops in
`localize2` on that combination.
The calculator reports those cases as unavailable instead of returning zero or
state left by an earlier step.

# Compute stress in a periodic cell
All three `pbc` flags true send `atoms.cell` to the library as the periodic
cell:

from ase import Atoms
from cpmdc.ase import CPMDCCalculator

water = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.1173], [0.0, 0.7572, -0.4692], [0.0, -0.7572, -0.4692]]
atoms = Atoms("OHH", positions=water, cell=[10.0, 10.0, 10.0], pbc=True)
with CPMDCCalculator("water.periodic.bin") as calc:
    atoms.calc = calc
    print(atoms.get_stress())
    print(atoms.get_stress(voigt=False))

Units are ASE's: positions and cells in Angstrom, energies in eV, forces in
eV/Angstrom, stress in eV/Angstrom^3, and dipole in e*Angstrom.
The calculator converts from the library's Hartree and Bohr with `HARTREE_TO_EV`
and `BOHR_TO_ANGSTROM`, which are the CODATA 2018 values.
ASE's default `ase.units` are CODATA 2014, so a number converted back with
`ase.units.Hartree` differs by about 1e-8 relative.
From ASE 3.24, `ase.units.create_units("2018")` agrees to 1e-10.
ASE 3.23 stores `mu0 = 4*pi*1e-7` in that table, the permeability from before
the 2019 SI revision, so the Bohr and Hartree it derives differ from these
constants by about 1e-9.
The calculator uses `HARTREE_TO_EV` and `BOHR_TO_ANGSTROM` on every ASE version.
Stress has ASE's sign: the derivative of the energy with respect to strain,
divided by the volume.
It is positive when the energy rises as the cell expands.
A tensor that is not exactly symmetric gives each shear component as the mean of
its two off-diagonal elements, as ASE's `full_3x3_to_voigt_6_stress` does.
The library returns the tensor with the opposite sign, the OpenCPMD convention,
and the calculator negates it.

The `pbc` flags choose the boundaries:

| `atoms.pbc` and `atoms.cell` | Step | Stress |
|------------------------------+------+--------|
| all false | no cell is sent: the deck sets the box and the Poisson solver, and `atoms.cell` is ignored | raises `PropertyNotImplementedError` |
| all true, three independent cell vectors | `atoms.cell` is sent as the periodic cell | computed when the deck is periodic |
| all true, fewer than three independent cell vectors | raises `ValueError` | |
| a mix of true and false | raises `ValueError` that names the open axes | |

A periodic cell with an isolated deck, such as `water.params.bin`, gives the
energy and the forces.
Asking that step for stress raises `PropertyNotImplementedError` with the
reason, and the calculator does not evaluate the step again to find it out.

# Relax a structure
This relaxes the positions of the isolated water and writes a trajectory:

from ase import Atoms
from ase.io import read
from ase.optimize import BFGS
from cpmdc.ase import CPMDCCalculator

water = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.1173], [0.0, 0.7572, -0.4692], [0.0, -0.7572, -0.4692]]
atoms = Atoms("OHH", positions=water)
atoms.calc = CPMDCCalculator("water.params.bin")
with BFGS(atoms, trajectory="water.traj", logfile=None) as opt:
    opt.run(fmax=0.01)
frames = read("water.traj", index=":")
print(len(frames), frames[-1].get_potential_energy())
print(frames[-1].calc.parameters)
atoms.calc.close()

Each frame of the trajectory stores the energy, the forces, the stress when the
step had one, and the calculator parameters, so `read` returns them without the
library.

With the periodic message, a cell filter relaxes the cell on the stress as well.
`constant_cutoff=` gives the stress the cell needs, as the end of this section
explains:

from ase import Atoms
from ase.filters import FrechetCellFilter
from ase.optimize import BFGS
from cpmdc.ase import CPMDCCalculator

water = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.1173], [0.0, 0.7572, -0.4692], [0.0, -0.7572, -0.4692]]
atoms = Atoms("OHH", positions=water, cell=[10.0, 10.0, 10.0], pbc=True)
atoms.rattle(0.05, seed=17)
with CPMDCCalculator("water.periodic.bin", constant_cutoff=30.0) as calc:
    atoms.calc = calc
    with BFGS(FrechetCellFilter(atoms), logfile=None) as opt:
        opt.run(fmax=0.01, steps=80)
    print(opt.nsteps, atoms.get_volume(), atoms.cell.lengths())

On the reference evaluator the minimum puts every atom at the origin, because
the well is anchored there and has no repulsion.
The reference energy is not translation invariant for the same reason.
The cell filter then shrinks the cell along y and z, the axes along which the
atoms sit off the origin.
These runs check that forces and stress reach the optimizer; the reference well
is not a chemical model.
On OpenCPMD each new cell starts a cold SCF with the full CPMD setup, as
Wavefunction state between calls (file:../explanation/wavefunction-state.org)
explains, so a cell relaxation costs more per step than a relaxation of the
positions.
A constant-cutoff deck under `CPMDC_CELL_IN_PLACE` moves a nearby cell in place
and stays warm instead.
Without `constant_cutoff`, the OpenCPMD stress at the 40 Ry cutoff of
`water.periodic.bin` is almost all Pulay stress, about 16 eV divided by the cell
volume, which is 0.016 eV/Angstrom^3 in the 10 Angstrom cube.
It is the derivative at a fixed number of plane waves, while each new cell
evaluates a fixed cutoff, so the cell filter shrinks the cell while the energy
rises: without `constant_cutoff` the run above falls below 250 Angstrom^3 in 9
steps, 0.8 eV above its start.
`constant_cutoff=30.0` keeps the 40 Ry basis and evaluates the constant-cutoff
functional at 30 Ry, whose stress follows the energy.
The run then converges at 919 Angstrom^3 in 53 steps, 0.85 eV below its start,
because one water has almost no intermolecular stress.
Relax a cell at a constant cutoff (file:constant-cutoff.org) explains the
parameters and gives the measured stress and volumes against the cutoff.

The reference well drawn by `docs/render_reference_well.py` is the shape of an
isolated one-atom step at a 70 Ry cutoff:

.. figure:: /_static/reference-well.svg
   :alt: Reference harmonic well, energy against displacement

   Reference well for one hydrogen atom. The script writes this figure
   from the evaluator formula.

The curve is zero at the origin and rises on both sides.

# Check the forces and the stress
ASE's finite differences test that the forces and the stress are derivatives of
the energy:

import numpy as np
from ase import Atoms
from ase.calculators.fd import calculate_numerical_forces, calculate_numerical_stress
from cpmdc.ase import CPMDCCalculator

water = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.1173], [0.0, 0.7572, -0.4692], [0.0, -0.7572, -0.4692]]
atoms = Atoms("OHH", positions=water, cell=[10.0, 10.0, 10.0], pbc=True)
atoms.rattle(0.05, seed=1)
with CPMDCCalculator("water.periodic.bin") as calc:
    atoms.calc = calc
    forces = calculate_numerical_forces(atoms, eps=1e-3)
    stress = calculate_numerical_stress(atoms, eps=1e-5)
    print(np.abs(atoms.get_forces() - forces).max())
    print(np.abs(atoms.get_stress() - stress).max())

The example evaluates 31 steps: two for each of the nine coordinates, two for
each of the six strain components, and the analytic step.
On the reference evaluator both differences are below 1e-13.
On OpenCPMD the SCF tolerance sets them.
At these steps the OpenCPMD runs of `tests/python/test_ase_calculator.py` allow
a force error of 2e-3 eV/Angstrom and a stress error of 1e-4 eV/Angstrom^3.

# Reuse a step
Results are cached as in ASE's own calculators.
A call on an unchanged structure returns the stored step.
A change of `positions`, `numbers`, `cell`, or `pbc` evaluates the structure
again, and `calc.calculation_required(atoms, properties)` returns true for such
a structure until it is evaluated.
A change of `initial_charges` or `initial_magmoms` evaluates the structure
again, because the calculator reads both; the next section says how.
A change of `tags`, `momenta`, `info`, or a constraint reuses the step as well,
because none of them is a system change: ASE applies a constraint to the forces
after the calculator returns them.
An equal copy of the `Atoms` gets the stored step from `get_property`.
`calc.reset()` clears the stored step and keeps the session open.
Calling `calc.calculate(atoms)` yourself evaluates the structure whatever is
stored, and replaces every stored result: a step that gives no stress does not
leave the stress of an earlier periodic step behind, and a step that fails
leaves nothing stored, so a later `get_potential_energy()` never returns the
energy of another structure.
Every step of a calculator, from `get_property` or from `calculate`, runs on the
same session while the atom count and the elemental composition stay the same.
`set()` with the value a parameter already has does not open a session.
`calc.get_property(name, atoms, allow_calculation=False)` returns the stored
value, or `None` when that structure has not been evaluated.

# Set the charge, the multiplicity, and the method
The `charge` and `multiplicity` fields of the `CPMDParams` message set the
charge and the spin, beside the functional, the cutoff, and the
pseudopotentials.
The calculator has no keyword for any of them.
It reads `atoms.initial_charges` and `atoms.initial_magmoms` as the ASE
calculators for GPAW, ORCA, NWChem, and Psi4 do, so a charged or spin-polarised
`Atoms` needs no second source of truth.

The total charge is `Q = sum(atoms.get_initial_charges())` and the total moment
is `M = sum(atoms.get_initial_magnetic_moments())`.
The moments are collinear, one per atom: an array of shape  with a
nonzero entry raises `ValueError`.
`Q` and `M` must be integers.
A sum counts as an integer when it lies within `n * eps * sum(|x|)` of one, the
bound on the rounding error of adding `n` float64 terms `x`, where `eps` is the
float64 unit roundoff; any other sum raises `ValueError` that names the sum.
The multiplicity is `|M| + 1`.

`cpmdc.params_method` reports the effective charge and multiplicity of the
message.
A multiplicity of 1 is the schema default, so the calculator takes it as unset
whether the message left the field out or wrote 1.
A charge of 0 is unset only when `hasCharge` is false on the value that wins.
That value is the top-level `charge` when no typed `system` charge is explicit,
and the typed `system` charge when `system.hasCharge` is true or that charge is
not 0.
Zero with `hasCharge` true is explicit.
The deck renderer and the Fortran embed record that same charge for the
message the session opens with.
Neither reads `Atoms.initial_charges`, and the C API does not read the
`ForceInput` charge fields.
The calculator decides the total before that handoff.
The sum of `initial_charges` is written into the top-level `charge` only when
the top-level `hasCharge` bit is false and the effective charge is still 0.
A typed section that still reports another charge after that write is refused
before a session opens.

Each of the two settings follows these rules:

| `Atoms` value | message value | result |
|--------+--------+--------|
| zero | any | the message value; nothing changes for an existing script |
| nonzero | unset | the `Atoms` value, written into the top-level `charge` or `multiplicity` field of the message the session opens with |
| nonzero | equal | the shared value, silently |
| nonzero | set and different | `ValueError` that names both values and both sources, `Atoms.initial_charges` or `Atoms.initial_magmoms` and the `CPMDParams` message in `params`; the set value is kept and the step is refused |

An explicit charge of 0 (`hasCharge` true) is a set value.
A nonzero `Atoms` total raises `ValueError`, and the charge stays 0.
A multiplicity of 1 has no such flag on `CPMDParams`, so a nonzero moment
replaces a multiplicity of 1.
A message whose typed `system` section fixes the charge, including
`system.hasCharge` `true` with charge 0, keeps that value.
The calculator raises `ValueError` before the step runs.
A message that `cpmdc_params_method()` refuses as ambiguous, because a raw
`&SYSTEM` block or a `SYSTEM.` set directive holds the scalar, raises
`CPMDCError` the first time an `Atoms` value needs it.

A change of `initial_charges` or `initial_magmoms` discards the stored results,
and the next call evaluates the structure again.
The calculator opens a new session only when the effective charge or
multiplicity changes; moving the charge from one atom to another keeps the
session.
`todict()` and `Parameters.write` hold only `params`, `library`, and
`constant_cutoff`, because the charge and the spin travel with the `Atoms`.

This example evaluates a water cation with a doublet spin, and shows the error
for partial charges, which are not a total charge:

from ase import Atoms
from cpmdc.ase import CPMDCCalculator

water = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.1173], [0.0, 0.7572, -0.4692], [0.0, -0.7572, -0.4692]]
cation = Atoms("OHH", positions=water)
cation.set_initial_charges([1.0, 0.0, 0.0])
cation.set_initial_magnetic_moments([1.0, 0.0, 0.0])
partial = Atoms("OHH", positions=water)
partial.set_initial_charges([0.5, 0.0, 0.0])
with CPMDCCalculator("water.params.bin") as calc:
    cation.calc = calc
    print(cation.get_potential_energy())
    partial.calc = calc
    try:
        partial.get_potential_energy()
    except ValueError as exc:
        print(exc)

A keyword such as `charge`, `multiplicity`, or `xc` raises `TypeError` in the
constructor and in `set()`, and the message names the key and points at
`params` and at the `Atoms` arrays.
To change the rest of the method, encode another message and pass it to
`set()`; this example switches to the periodic message:

from cpmdc.ase import CPMDCCalculator

try:
    CPMDCCalculator("water.params.bin", charge=-1)
except TypeError as exc:
    print(exc)
with CPMDCCalculator("water.params.bin") as calc:
    print(calc.set(params="water.periodic.bin"))
    print(calc.todict())

`set()` returns a dictionary of the parameters that changed, with their new
values.
A new `params`, `library`, or `constant_cutoff` opens a new session and clears
the stored results.
A value that cannot be opened raises and leaves the old session in use.

# Choose the working directory
Each step runs with `calc.directory` as the working directory of the process,
and the process returns to its own directory afterwards.
`directory` defaults to `"."`, which changes nothing.
`label="run/water"` sets `directory` to `"run"`, as it does for every ASE
calculator; the prefix, `water`, is unused.
ASE's `Calculator.calculate` creates the directory on the first step when it
does not exist.

Two relative paths resolve against `directory`:

- a relative `CPMDC_PSEUDO_DIR` or `CPMD_PP_LIBRARY_PATH`, read on the first
  step of each session, so give an absolute path when calculators run in more
  than one directory;
- the `RESTART.1` that a deck with `RESTART WAVEFUNCTION` reads on a cold start,
  unless the message sets `permanentDir` or `scratchDir`, which CPMD then works
  in.

A library step writes no `RESTART.1`, `LATEST`, `GEOMETRY`, or `GEOMETRY.xyz`,
and the orbitals for the next step stay in memory.
`params` is read when it is set, relative to the directory of the process at
that moment, not to `directory`.
`calc.parameters` keeps that file, and a `library` path, as an absolute path,
so a copy that opens its session in another directory and a calculator rebuilt
from `calc.todict()` there use the same files.
The `restart` argument is deprecated and ignored, and passing it warns with
`DeprecationWarning`.

The working directory belongs to the process, so another thread that opens a
relative path during a step opens it under `directory`.
Calls into the library must already come from one thread at a time, because it
keeps one CPMD state per process, as the C ABI reference (file:../reference/c-abi.org)
says.

# Handle errors
| Condition | Raised |
|-----------+--------|
| a step that the library rejects, such as one without a pseudopotential directory, or one whose energy, forces, or stress is NaN or infinite | `cpmdc.ase.CalculationFailed` |
| a keyword other than `params`, `library`, `constant_cutoff`, and ASE's own; no `params` | `TypeError` |
| stress or dipole where the step has none; `energies`, `magmoms`, or `charges` | `ase.calculators.calculator.PropertyNotImplementedError` |
| mixed `pbc` flags, a periodic cell of rank below 3 (the numpy.linalg.matrix_rank cutoff), or a cell volume below the normal float64 range | `ValueError` |
| a step on a calculator without atoms | `ValueError` |
| a `params` file that does not exist | `FileNotFoundError` |

`CalculationFailed` is both ASE's `CalculationFailed` and `cpmdc.CPMDCError`, so
code that catches either one for another calculator catches it unchanged.
Its message names the working directory of the step and gives the library's
reason.
The calculator stays usable, and the next call evaluates the step again.

# Sessions and copies
`session_accept_topology` fixes the topology only after an evaluation call
passes its argument checks and collective orbital preflight. A rejected
preflight leaves the topology configurable.
A reordering of the same atoms stays on the session.
After a successful step, a structure with another composition closes the
session and opens a new one from the same `params`.

`calc.parameters` holds `params`, `library`, and `constant_cutoff`, with
absolute paths.
`calc.todict()` returns them for a trajectory or a database row.
A `params` buffer given as bytes is encoded as standard Base64 under
`{"cpmdparams_base64": ...}`, so the dictionary stays JSON data and still
rebuilds the same calculator.
`CPMDCCalculator(**calc.todict())` builds an equal calculator in any working
directory, and `CPMDCCalculator(parameters="calc.ase")` reads a file written by
`calc.parameters.write("calc.ase")`.

ASE rebuilds a calculator from `calc.name` and `calc.todict()`, in a trajectory,
an `ase.db` row, and `PythonSubProcessCalculator`, and asks no pickling of a
calculator.
`copy.copy`, `copy.deepcopy`, and `pickle`, which `copy.deepcopy(atoms)` and
`ase.visualize.view` use, keep the parameters and the stored results, and the
copy opens its own session on its first step.
`close()` closes the session, and the next step opens a new one.
The calculator is a context manager that closes on exit.

`calc.read(label)` always raises ASE's `ReadError`, because a step stores no file
that holds results, and ASE's default would only set the label and let the
caller think that results were restored.
The `restart` keyword stays deprecated and ignored, as the reference page says.
`parameters=` is the supported way to load a saved calculator.

`ase.calculators.mixing.SumCalculator` takes several `CPMDCCalculator` objects,
or one beside another ASE calculator, and evaluates each one once per
structure.
Its stress for a cluster raises `PropertyNotImplementedError`, as the
calculator's own does.

# Check the calculator with ASE
`tests/python/test_ase_conformance.py` asks of `CPMDCCalculator` what any ASE
user asks of a calculator, and answers with ASE's own tools.
It runs on the default build, which needs no OpenCPMD archive.
`pixi run test-stub` builds it, and
`pixi run pytest tests/python/test_ase_conformance.py`
runs the file.
The file checks these points:

| Question | ASE tool |
|----------+----------|
| `implemented_properties` lists energy, free energy, forces, stress, and dipole, and a stored step has ASE's shapes | `calc.results`, `ase.io.write` and `read` of extended XYZ |
| a property outside the list raises, without evaluating a step | `PropertyNotImplementedError`, `get_charges()`, `get_magnetic_moment()` |
| the stored step is reused and discarded as ASE expects | `check_state`, `system_changes`, `calculation_required`, `get_property(..., allow_calculation=False)` |
| a changed `params`, `library`, or `constant_cutoff` discards the stored step | `set`, `calculation_required` |
| later changes to the caller's `Atoms` leave the stored structure as it was | `calc.atoms`, `get_atoms` |
| the results survive a trajectory, extended XYZ through `SinglePointCalculator`, and an `ase.db` row, which rebuilds the calculator in another directory | `ase.io`, `ase.db`, `todict` |
| a run of steps keeps one session | a count of the `Session` objects opened |
| a rejected step is `ase.calculators.calculator.CalculationFailed` with the library's message | a real library error, not a mock |
| a relaxation runs with a constraint | `BFGS` with `FixAtoms` |
| `read` refuses, and a refused `read` leaves the calculator as it was | `ReadError`, `CalculatorError` |
| state outside the system changes, and an equal copy of the structure, keep the stored step | `check_state`, `Atoms.copy` |
| the parameters round trip through `todict` and a `Parameters` file, including a `constant_cutoff` mapping | `Parameters.write`, `parameters=` |
| two calculators add up and each runs once per structure | `SumCalculator` |
| a molecular dynamics run conserves the energy and evaluates once per move | `VelocityVerlet` |
| copies and pickles work, with or without the `params` file | `copy`, `pickle` |
| energies are in eV, forces in eV/Angstrom, stress in eV/Angstrom^3 | `ase.units`, `calculate_numerical_forces`, `calculate_numerical_stress` |
| each Voigt stress component has the sign and the size of a central difference of the energy over strain, taken in the test | `Atoms.set_cell(..., scale_atoms=True)` |
| a few steps of a cell relaxation lower the energy and the largest stress component | `BFGS` with `FrechetCellFilter` |

`cpmdc.lammps.FixExternal` follows the same conventions where it shares them: the
same units, a failed step reported as `CPMDCError`, a step with a NaN or infinite
result refused, and a new session opened after a change of composition even when
the previous attempt to open one failed.


## File: docs/orgmode/howto/check-forces.org

# Goal
Compare the forces a session returns with central differences of its
energy, the way the CP2K `DEBUG` run type does with `DEBUG_FORCES` and
`DEBUG_STRESS_TENSOR`.
A mismatch points at the gradient, not at the energy.

# Run the check
`cpmdc-fd-check` is built with the tests (`-Dwith_tests=true`) and is not
installed.
It takes one `CPMDParams` message and one `ForceInput` step:

build/cpmdc-fd-check build/water_blyp_params.bin build/force_input_water.bin

Each coordinate moves by `+DX` and `-DX` Bohr, so a check of `N` atoms
costs `6N` energy evaluations after the first one.
Every evaluation is a `cpmdc_session_calculate_result()` call with
`lengthUnit = "bohr"` and `energyUnit = "hartree"`.
The numerical force is `-(E(+DX) - E(-DX)) / (2 DX)`.

| Option | Default | CP2K keyword |
|--------+---------+--------------|
| `--dx` | `1e-3` Bohr | `DEBUG%DX` |
| `--max-relative-error` | `0.2` percent | `DEBUG%MAX_RELATIVE_ERROR` |
| `--eps-no-error-check` | `1e-5` a.u. | `DEBUG%EPS_NO_ERROR_CHECK` |
| `--stress` | off | `DEBUG%DEBUG_STRESS_TENSOR` |

A component whose analytic value is below `--eps-no-error-check` is printed
and not checked.
A force at or below `1e-4` Hartree/Bohr may be off by five times the limit.
The last line of each block gives the largest absolute and relative error and
how many components were checked.
The exit status is 0 when every checked component agrees, 1 on a mismatch,
and 2 on a usage, input, or evaluation error.

# Check the stress
`--stress` needs a periodic cell for which the calculator writes
`PotentialResult.stress`; an isolated cell exits with status 2.
Each of the six symmetric strains `eps_ab` is applied as `+DX` and `-DX` to
the cell vectors and to the positions, so the fractional coordinates stay
fixed.
That costs 12 more evaluations.
The check compares virials in Hartree, as CP2K compares `pv_virial`, so
`--eps-no-error-check` means the same as there.
The numerical virial is `-(E(+DX) - E(-DX)) / (2 DX)` and the analytic one
is the volume times `PotentialResult.stress` in Hartree/Bohr^3, the sign of
OpenCPMD `paiu/omega`.

# What the reference build shows
The reference evaluator returns the analytic gradient of its energy, so its
forces agree to rounding.
Its stress is `-dE/d(eps) / volume`, the OpenCPMD sign of that derivative,
so `--stress` agrees to rounding as well.
An isolated cell still has no tensor.

# With OpenCPMD
An SCF energy carries the error of its convergence.
Converge the orbitals well below `DX` times the force you want to check, or
the differences measure the SCF threshold instead of the gradient.


## File: docs/orgmode/howto/constant-cutoff.org

# Goal
Give an ASE cell filter, a LAMMPS `fix box/relax` or `fix npt`, or GROMACS
pressure coupling a stress that follows the energy of a periodic OpenCPMD deck.
Turn on the constant-cutoff kinetic functional of [[https://doi.org/10.1016/0022-3697(94)00228-2][Bernasconi et al., J. Phys.
Chem. Solids 56, 501 (1995)]],
which OpenCPMD reads as `CONSTANT CUTOFF` in `&SYSTEM`.
It is off by default, and a message without it renders the same deck as before.

# Why a fixed cutoff misleads a cell optimizer
OpenCPMD's stress is the derivative of the energy at a fixed set of plane waves.
A new cell is a new setup of the deck at the same cutoff, which holds a
different set, so the energy of the next cell is not the energy the stress
predicted.
The difference is the Pulay stress.
On the 40 Ry periodic water deck it is about 16 eV divided by the volume, 1.6e-2
eV/Angstrom^3 in the 10 Angstrom cube, and it grows as the cell shrinks: a cell
filter shrinks the cell while the energy rises.

The functional replaces G^2 in the kinetic energy by

G^2 + A [1 + erf((G^2 - E0) / sigma)]

with A, sigma, and E0 in Ry.
A plane wave above E0 costs up to 2A more, so the orbitals hold almost no weight
above E0 in any cell, and the energy belongs to the constant cutoff E0 while the
basis keeps the cutoff of the deck.
`kin_energy`, `vpsi`, and the kinetic stress of OpenCPMD apply the term and its
derivative, so the stress is the derivative of that energy.
The OpenCPMD manual prints the argument of erf as `G^2 / 2 - E0 / sigma`; the
code in `kin_energy_utils.mod.F90` uses `(G^2 - E0) / sigma`.

# From ASE or Python
Pass E0 in Ry:

from ase import Atoms
from ase.filters import FrechetCellFilter
from ase.optimize import BFGS
from cpmdc.ase import CPMDCCalculator

water = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.1173], [0.0, 0.7572, -0.4692], [0.0, -0.7572, -0.4692]]
atoms = Atoms("OHH", positions=water, cell=[10.0, 10.0, 10.0], pbc=True)
atoms.rattle(0.05, seed=17)
with CPMDCCalculator("water.periodic.bin", constant_cutoff=30.0) as calc:
    atoms.calc = calc
    with BFGS(FrechetCellFilter(atoms), logfile=None) as opt:
        opt.run(fmax=0.01, steps=80)
    print(opt.nsteps, atoms.get_volume())

The keyword also takes a mapping or a `cpmdc.ConstantCutoff` that sets A or
sigma.
For example, `ConstantCutoff(30.0, height_ry=2000.0, width_ry=3.0)` sets both.
`UnitCellFilter` and `ase.md.npt.NPT` read the same stress.
`Session` and `Potential` take the same keyword.
`calc.set(constant_cutoff=...)` opens a new session; `None` turns the functional
off.

# From a message: LAMMPS, GROMACS, i-PI, and C
Hosts that read a `CPMDParams` file take the functional from the `system`
section of the message, with A, sigma, and E0 in that order:

( system = ( symmetry = 1, angstrom = true, cutOffRy = 40.0,
    cell = [10.0, 1.0, 1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0],
    constantCutoff = [2000.0, 3.0, 30.0] ) ),

`pair_style cpmdc`, `cpmdc.lammps.FixExternal`, `libcpmdc_gromacs`, and the
socket drivers then evaluate it.
A C host can set it on a session before its first step instead:

CPMDCSession *s = cpmdc_session_create(params_bytes, params_size);
if (!s || cpmdc_session_set_constant_cutoff(s, 30.0, 0.0, 0.0) != 0)
  fprintf(stderr, "%s\n", cpmdc_last_error());

A height or width of 0 selects the defaults below.
A job TOML for `tools/job_toml.py` takes a `[constant_cutoff]` table with
`cutoff_ry`, and optionally `height_ry` and `width_ry`.

# Choose E0, A, and sigma
- E0 + 2 sigma must not exceed the cutoff of the deck; `cpmdc` refuses the
  setting otherwise, with the three numbers in the message.
  Keep the deck cutoff a little above E0, for example E0 = 30 Ry on a 40 Ry
  deck.
- Without A, `cpmdc` uses 50 times the deck cutoff; without sigma, E0 / 10.
  The penalty then rises from near 0 at E0 - 2 sigma to 2A at E0 + 2 sigma.
- A larger A brings the stress closer to dE/dV, but a very large A reaches below
  E0 through the tail of erf and moves the energy itself.
- Converge the physics in E0, not in the deck cutoff.
  The energy is that of a basis a little below E0, so it lies above the energy
  of the plain deck: -443.69 eV for the water at E0 = 30 Ry on the 40 Ry deck,
  against -459.24 eV for the plain 40 Ry deck.
  Compare energies only at the same E0, A, and sigma.
- A message that gives `&SYSTEM` as raw text, or that already sets
  `system.constantCutoff`, cannot take `constant_cutoff=` as well.

Without `tools/opencpmd_constant_cutoff_precon.patch` the ODIIS preconditioner
ignores the penalty, ODIIS stops at its step limit, and `cpmdc` continues with
PCG, which is slower; the archive how-to (file:opencpmd-archive.org) lists
the patch.

# Measured on the water deck
`bench/constant_cutoff_scan.py` ran the periodic water deck at four basis
cutoffs, as written and with E0 = 0.75 times the cutoff and the default A and
sigma, on an Intel Xeon virtual machine with 8 vCPUs.
The full output is in `bench/results/constant_cutoff_water.org`.
The first table compares the analytic mean stress of the unrelaxed water with
dE/dV between two cells strained isotropically by 1.5%, and gives the mean wall
time of those three stress calls:

| Cutoff, Ry | E0, Ry | Mean stress, eV/A^3 | dE/dV, eV/A^3 | Difference, eV/A^3 | Time per stress call, s |
|-+-+-+-+-+-|
| 25 | - | +2.065e-02 | -1.801e-03 | +2.25e-02 | 1.7 |
| 25 | 18.75 | -3.720e-03 | -3.932e-03 | +2.12e-04 | 1.7 |
| 40 | - | +1.587e-02 | -6.389e-04 | +1.65e-02 | 2.7 |
| 40 | 30 | -3.535e-03 | -3.659e-03 | +1.23e-04 | 3.6 |
| 60 | - | +6.461e-03 | -4.789e-04 | +6.94e-03 | 4.7 |
| 60 | 45 | -1.826e-03 | -1.855e-03 | +2.91e-05 | 6.2 |
| 80 | - | +1.511e-03 | -3.334e-04 | +1.84e-03 | 8.2 |
| 80 | 60 | -5.923e-04 | -6.229e-04 | +3.06e-05 | 10.1 |

At a fixed cutoff the stress exceeds the slope of the energy by 2.25e-2
eV/Angstrom^3 at 25 Ry and still by 1.84e-3 eV/Angstrom^3 at 80 Ry.
At a constant cutoff it is below 2.2e-4 eV/Angstrom^3 and follows the sign of
the slope; the stress that remains is the internal stress of the unrelaxed
bonds.
A stress call costs 1.0 to 1.33 times as much as at the fixed cutoff.

The second table relaxes the water rattled by 0.05 Angstrom with BFGS on a
`FrechetCellFilter`, to fmax 0.01 eV/Angstrom or 80 steps, and stops when the
cell falls below a quarter of its 1000 Angstrom^3:

| Cutoff, Ry | E0, Ry | Result | Steps | Final volume, A^3 | Final mean stress, eV/A^3 | Energy change, eV | Steps that raise the energy | Wall time, s |
|-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-+-|
| 25 | - | collapsed | 9 | 219.5 | - | -0.012 | 6 | 9 |
| 25 | 18.75 | converged | 18 | 940.1 | -2.0e-06 | -1.249 | 0 | 33 |
| 40 | - | collapsed | 9 | 226.1 | - | +0.797 | 8 | 16 |
| 40 | 30 | converged | 53 | 919.1 | +4.2e-06 | -0.851 | 20 | 192 |
| 60 | - | collapsed | 10 | 220.3 | - | +0.810 | 8 | 37 |
| 60 | 45 | converged | 12 | 998.1 | +5.3e-07 | -0.337 | 0 | 83 |
| 80 | - | collapsed | 12 | 223.0 | - | +0.874 | 9 | 68 |
| 80 | 60 | converged | 14 | 989.6 | +1.8e-05 | -0.220 | 0 | 144 |

At every fixed cutoff the cell collapses within 12 steps, and from 40 Ry up the
energy ends higher than it started.
At a constant cutoff every run converges between 919 and 998 Angstrom^3: one
water in a 10 Angstrom box has almost no intermolecular stress.
At 40 Ry, BFGS overshoots on that flat volume mode, so 20 of its 53 steps raise
the energy, by at most 0.041 eV; the first six steps lower it every time.

Density of water at a constant cutoff (file:../explanation/constant-cutoff-npt.org)
runs NPT dynamics of 32 waters with and without the functional and compares
the density with a published PBE value.

The C ABI (file:../reference/c-abi.org), Python API (file:../reference/python.org),
and CPMD options (file:../reference/cpmd-options.org) references list the
call, the keyword, and the message field.


## File: docs/orgmode/howto/debug-deck.org

# Goal
See the CPMD input deck that `cpmdc` renders from a `CPMDParams` message, and
work out what the OpenCPMD path changes before CPMD (Car-Parrinello Molecular
Dynamics) parses it.

# Write the deck to a file
Set `CPMDC_DECK_OUT` to a file name before the process configures `cpmdc`:

export CPMDC_DECK_OUT=$PWD/method.inp
build/example_host_step params.bin step.bin
cat method.inp

`cpmdc` writes the file each time it renders a message: in
`cpmdc_session_create()`, `cpmdc_session_set_params()`, `cpmdc_set_params()`,
the `PotentialConfig` entry points, and every one-shot call.
Each write replaces the previous content, so the file holds the deck of the
most recent configuration.
The write happens in the default build too, so a message can be checked on a
machine without OpenCPMD.
An empty `CPMDC_DECK_OUT`, or a path that cannot be opened for writing,
skips the write without an error.

Under `mpirun` every rank renders the same deck to the same path.
Point each rank at its own file when the ranks share a file system, for
example through a wrapper script that appends `$OMPI_COMM_WORLD_RANK`.

# What the OpenCPMD path changes
The file holds the method deck.
On each cold evaluation, the OpenCPMD path builds the deck that
CPMD parses from it in three steps:

1. If the method deck has an `&ATOMS` block with coordinate lines, it is used
   as it is.
   Otherwise every `&ATOMS` block is dropped and a new one is written from the
   step's atomic numbers and positions.
   A `!SPECIES SYM` comment in the method deck selects that element's file,
   `LMAX`, `LOC`, and, when the `*file` line has it, `KLEINMAN-BYLANDER`.
   An element with no such comment uses the built-in table (see
   writing a CPMDParams message (file:write-cpmdparams.org)).
   An element in neither fails before CPMD starts, and the error names the
   atomic number.
   When the method deck has no `&CPMD`, `&SYSTEM`, or `&DFT` section at all,
   a minimal deck replaces it: `OPTIMIZE WAVEFUNCTION`,
   `CONVERGENCE ORBITALS 1.0d-5`, `MAXITER 40`, `ANGSTROM`, and the
   functional, cutoff, charge, and multiplicity of the message.
   The symmetry comes from the step's box.
   A cube is `SYMMETRY 1`.
   Unequal orthogonal edges are `SYMMETRY 8`.
   A tilted box is `CELL VECTORS` with no `SYMMETRY` line.
